entry.evidence: We present an approach for extracting quantifiable information from archival aerial photographs to extend the temporal record of change

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text) and published PDF

steps.action: Frame the problem: few studies of the many small Greenland outlets, the assumption that they change homogeneously, and sparse pre-1972 data.
steps.quote: it had been tempting to infer that change in this multitude of relatively poorly studied smaller outlets was homogeneous

steps.action: Propose Structure-from-Motion processing of the 1930-31 BAARE oblique survey photographs into georeferenced orthophotos, supplemented by 1966 CORONA and 1981 aerial imagery.
steps.quote: we utilize Structure from Motion (SfM) approaches to build georeferenced orthophotos of the terrain within the BAARE imagery

steps.action: Assemble the three archival photo sets: 73 surviving BAARE plates, 1966 CORONA KH-4 stereo images, and 58 vertical aerial images from 1981.
steps.quote: For our study, we used 73 images obtained during the summers of 1930 and 1931.

steps.action: Choose the ArcticDEM 2 m mosaic over the day-stamped strips as ground truth for GCPs on stable bare ground, removing visible mosaic artefacts.
steps.quote: Thus we decided to use the 2 m mosaic.

steps.action: Characterize orthophotomap georeferencing accuracy (GCP error about 1 pixel, under 20 m spatially; Table 1) and bound GCP isostatic uplift (at most 18 cm) as negligible.
steps.quote: The GCP placement accuracy calculated during the processing of the mosaics was around 1 pixel

steps.action: Add low-cloud July-August Landsat 5/7/8 composites for 1985, 1995, 2005, 2015 and 2019.
steps.quote: we use satellite records to explore glacier change from 1985 to the present day

steps.action: Delineate margins manually at seven epochs, measure centre-line length change as rates in m per year, and propagate orthomosaic accuracy into RMSE errors per time step.
steps.quote: Based on this information we calculate RMSE errors for distance measurements

steps.action: Take forcing records from other groups: Tasiilaq air temperature and PDD, HadISST SST, modelled SE Greenland SMB (all against a 1951-1980 baseline), and Kangerlussuaq Fjord bathymetry.
steps.quote: subsequent investigations and analyses also make use of a range of additional environmental datasets

steps.action: Report frontal changes: net retreat of all glaciers over 1930-2019 (Fig. 3), retreat in 1930-66, advance in 1985-95, and accelerated retreat in 2015-19 (Figs. 4-5, Table 2).
steps.quote: over this time period all glaciers in our study area experienced overall retreat

steps.action: Split glaciers by type in box plots to establish a common retreat-advance-retreat pattern, larger variability in marine-terminating glaciers, and some stable glaciers.
steps.quote: These plots reveal that there is substantial variability between individual glaciers

steps.action: Describe the air temperature, PDD, SST and SMB series relative to their baselines at the times of the glacier observations (Fig. 7).
steps.quote: SSTs very closely track changes in annual air temperatures

steps.action: Pose climatic forcing (accumulation, flow, melt and calving balance) as the candidate driver of the terminus changes.
steps.quote: in an effort to explore likely drivers for the changes in ice front positions that we observe in the archival imagery

steps.action: Divide the forcing record into cool-warm-cool-warm periods and compare them qualitatively with the SMB and frontal response, noting lags and the absence of simple tracking.
steps.quote: We also observe these external forcings playing out in the changing extent of the outlets, but with a degree of complexity

steps.action: Retain the claim that regional trends track climatic forcing, while qualifying Hanna et al. (2021) on flat recent temperature trends.
steps.quote: do track the prevailing climatic forcing

steps.action: Hypothesize, following Wood et al. (2021), that warming ocean waters contribute to the observed loss, while noting that no subsurface temperature data are available.
steps.quote: We hypothesize that warming ocean waters may well play an important role in the mass loss we observe.

steps.action: Compare the type-dependent response (marine-terminating more dynamic and variable) with published work that documents the same behaviour.
steps.quote: The marine-terminating glaciers in our study region are (a) more dynamic, (b) show more retreat, and (c) show more varied behaviour

steps.action: Propose that the recent larger changes of land-terminating and local glaciers reflect SMB becoming a stronger driver.
steps.quote: We propose that this “switch” could be representative of SMB becoming an increasingly important driver of change in recent years

steps.action: Establish that neighbouring glaciers of the same type, under the same forcing, respond very differently.
steps.quote: we also observe significant local heterogeneity in glacier response

steps.action: List non-climatic rival controls: ice velocity, ocean circulation, bed topography and bathymetry, sea ice, and ice thickness.
steps.quote: glacier response is defined not only by climatic variables (e.g. air temperature, SST) but also by (a) ice velocity

steps.action: Examine margins of Glaciers 7-10 and 14-15 (Figs. 8-9): most outlets are stable, while Glacier 8's southern outlets, Glacier 10 and Glacier 15 show large or stepped retreat.
steps.quote: there are three outlets that in particular show 2–3 times more retreat than these

steps.action: Adopt Wood et al.'s explanation: stable glaciers sit on shallow pinning ridges, and retreat episodes mark glaciers moving off ridges into deeper water.
steps.quote: we propose that these understudied glaciers also sit on ridges and/or in shallow water

steps.action: Compare bathymetry in front of Glacier 14 with its terminus behaviour: water is deeper in front of the stable part, which is contrary to a simple shallow-water expectation.
steps.quote: This reveals starkly different topography, with that in front of the more stable region being significantly deeper

steps.action: Keep the pinning-ridge hypothesis by reinterpreting a subtle bed shallowing directly at the western terminus as a pinning ridge.
steps.quote: directly in front of the western part of this glacier, there is a subtle shallowing of the bed

steps.action: Offer a rival in which high ice velocities offset calving (Glacier 14 west) or fail to offset it (Glacier 14 east, Glacier 15), using Joughin et al. velocities.
steps.quote: comparatively high calving rates are offset by higher ice velocities delivering ice more rapidly to the ice front

steps.action: Compare with published studies (Porter et al. 2018b; Catania et al. 2018) that find local and geometric controls dominate, and note this record is three times longer.
steps.quote: Similar to our findings, they also showed that taking account of the presence of shallow sills was important

steps.action: Keep the claim that non-photogrammetric archival imagery yields quantitative glacier-change data.
steps.quote: Our investigation has shown the potential of archival imagery

steps.action: Keep the claim that climate forcing controls the regional trends, with SST arguably more important for water-terminating outlets.
steps.quote: climate forcing exhibits strong controls on glaciers in the region generally

steps.action: Keep the headline claim of large glacier-to-glacier heterogeneity, with shallow pinning ridges proposed as the control of marine-terminating variability.
steps.quote: one of our primary conclusions is that there is enormous variability in how glaciers respond to the climatic and non-climatic drivers

steps.action: Asked by RC1 why later warm periods produced more retreat than the 1930s-40s, the authors answer with bed topography and add the earlier-versus-later warm period argument to §4.2 ¶7.
steps.quote: is a demonstration of just how important bed topography is

steps.action: Reword the framing of past regional studies (Study area, Conclusions) as investigations of broad-scale patterns, at the request of RC1 and RC2.
steps.quote: we have modified the manuscript to follow the first of the two alternative suggestions made

steps.action: Decline to add observation errors for SST and SMB, arguing that combined, cross-validated products have no meaningful per-observation error.
steps.quote: it’s not clear that a meaningful “observation error” can be provided

steps.action: After RC1 questioned the Glacier 14 interpretation, add a possible pinning ridge from bed shallowing, keep the velocity alternative, and tone down confidence.
steps.quote: We have now added some text to suggest that there may well be a shallowing in the bathymetry

steps.action: Remove the unsupported surface-thinning and greatest-mass-loss statements for Glacier 15 and replace them with a velocity-plus-retreat inference.
steps.quote: we have removed this statement about losing the greatest amount of mass and surface thinning

steps.action: Decline to move the lag-identification paragraph of §3.5 to the Discussion.
steps.quote: we believe that there is a strong rationale for keeping its current position

steps.action: Soften the stated contradiction with Hanna et al. (2021) on contemporary temperature trends into a qualification, and add a PDD discussion.
steps.quote: We therefore modify our text to reduce the significance of the apparent conflict between Hanna et al. (2021) and us.

steps.action: Downgrade the claim that warming waters are responsible for tidewater retreat to a hypothesis.
steps.quote: We do not know that warming waters are responsible, but rather we hypothesise that warming waters may well be influential.

steps.action: Decline to move the descriptive heterogeneity paragraph (Glaciers 8, 10, 14, 15) from the Discussion to the Results.
steps.quote: we prefer to leave it in its current position

steps.action: Clarify for RC2 that GCPs enter the SfM step (masking, GCP reprojection check and removal) and promise a workflow description and diagram.
steps.quote: orthomosaics are georeferenced as part of the SfM processing pipeline, not as an independent step afterwards

steps.action: Decline to use the existing 1980s orthophoto with in-situ GCPs (Korsgaard et al. 2016), for consistency of pipeline and reference model.
steps.quote: we wanted to use the same processing pipeline and reference model for all the data sets

steps.action: Promise to remove the uninformative 3D error from Table 1.
steps.quote: this 3D error does not carry significant information and will be removed from the next version of the manuscript

steps.action: Justify in the rebuttal, without adding selection criteria to the text, the inclusion of glaciers lacking 1930s data.
steps.quote: we did not want to limit our data set even further just in order to unify the time steps

steps.action: Remove mass-loss statements that were based only on retreat rates.
steps.quote: We have removed mention of mass loss where this was based on a reading of retreat rates.

tree.answer: Long-term frontal change of small East Greenland outlets and its heterogeneity
Yes; terminus positions are visible directly in archival orthophotos and Landsat images
Extend the record before the satellite era and identify drivers of change
Climatic drivers (air temperature, SST, SMB) versus local controls (bathymetric ridges, velocity, sea ice, thickness)
Only qualitatively; no distinct quantitative predictions are derived
Found, not set: opportunistic snapshots at seven epochs

tree.answer: Yes, 24 glaciers under shared forcing act as natural repetitions
Only accuracy checks (GCP error, uplift); interpretation not varied
Climate control of broad trends kept; ridge control proposed speculatively
Survived review after interpretation was toned down and Glacier 14/15 claims revised

end.claim: Over about 90 years, air and sea surface temperatures controlled the broad retreat-advance-retreat pattern of these East Greenland glaciers, but responses were strongly heterogeneous, and non-climatic controls, notably shallow pinning ridges in front of calving margins, best explain the variability.

decisive_move.sentence: Without SfM processing of the 1930s BAARE oblique plates (and 1966 CORONA) into georeferenced orthophotos, there would be no pre-satellite terminus record and hence no 90-year comparison.

gates.evidence: Action: the imagery was opportunistic ('make opportunistic use of this imagery', §0 ¶1), and bathymetry was used where it happened to exist (§4.2 ¶5). Claim: frontal rates could have failed to track the forcing periods (§4.1 ¶1), but the comparison is qualitative. The ridge hypothesis met data only at Glacier 14, where deeper water at the stable front was reinterpreted (§4.2 ¶5). Registration: nothing is stated as fixed in advance, apart from the inherited 1951-1980 baseline (§2.5.1 ¶1).

imports.item: Declassified CORONA KH-4 panoramic satellite imagery (1966)
British Arctic Air Route Expedition oblique survey photographs (1930-31)

novelty_claims.quote: this suite of data provides unprecedented insights into the changes that have taken place over > 90 years
This is unique to our study because this area is relatively little studied
The novelty of our work is not only the exploration of previously unstudied, smaller outlets in East Greenland
Our study covers ∼ 90 years and is the first such dedicated study in this region and over this duration.
we have shown such behaviour in a previously unstudied region of eastern Greenland

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: terminus change rates per glacier and time step are estimate_with_resolution (Table 2, §2.4 ¶1); the archival SfM pipeline is capability_characterized (§2.2 ¶2, §5 ¶1); climate tracking of regional trends is a qualitative regularity_in_range with no statistical test (§4.1 ¶1); the ridge control and the velocity-offset alternative are speculative hypotheses tested only at Glacier 14 (§4.2 ¶4-6). Process the document does not show: no correlation statistics between forcing and frontal rates are reported; air temperature comes from a single station, SST from a few grid cells, and SMB is a modelled regional mean; bathymetry exists only for Glacier 14 and Kangerlussuaq Fjord. The Figure 7c caption names Mittivakkat Gletscher, while §2.5.3 and §3.4 describe modelled SE Greenland SMB (inconsistency). RMSE distance errors of 26-39 m (§2.4 ¶1) are not obviously reconciled with the per-step rate errors in Table 2. Inference: the published Table 1 still lists 2D/3D errors although AC2 p.3 promised to remove the 3D error, and §5 ¶3 still speaks of 'greatest mass loss' despite AC2 p.5. The Supplement with processing details was not supplied. RC2's comment text is truncated in the record and is known mainly through AC2. Glacier selection criteria are not stated in the paper, and only 7 glaciers have 1930-1966 rates. The P step at Glacier 14 was referee-prompted according to AC1 p.6; it is coded from the published text in the final sequence.

disagreements.target: Inference from ice-sheet-wide analyses that small outlets change homogeneously (Moon et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: Neighbouring glaciers of the same type, under shared forcing, show very different 90-year frontal histories (Figs. 6, 8, 9).
disagreements.quote: This, however, is a significant oversight

disagreements.target: Regional-scale analyses of the Greenland Ice Sheet (Mouginot et al. 2019; King et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: Glacier-to-glacier heterogeneity within one region shows that regional aggregation masks variability.
disagreements.quote: Here, we suggest that even this approach masks important variability

disagreements.target: Hanna et al. (2021): Greenland air temperature trends generally flat since 2001
disagreements.support: Tasiilaq records, especially minimum temperatures, show an increasing trend over the contemporary period as a whole, though the post-2001 trend is subdued.
disagreements.quote: However, considering the contemporary period as a whole, we believe that temperature trends do show an overall increasing trend.

disagreements.target: Catania et al. (2018): fjord geometry controls on tidewater retreat in West Greenland over 30 years
disagreements.support: The same type of control is identified in unstudied East Greenland outlets over a record three times as long.
disagreements.quote: However, their work was focussed in West Greenland and explored changes over the [...] .

alternatives_considered.chosen: ArcticDEM 2 m DSM mosaic as ground-truth model for GCPs
alternatives_considered.reason: Strips often misaligned, prone to artefacts, incomplete, and captured at different times

alternatives_considered.chosen: Use all available images in SfM processing
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Select images with the best overlap or light conditions

alternatives_considered.chosen: Treat GCPs as fixed, ignoring isostatic uplift
alternatives_considered.reason: Uplift of 0-2 mm per year gives at most 18 cm over 90 years, small against other uncertainties
Manual approach found more suitable and more accurate

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both offered: pinning ridge from subtle bed shallowing, and high velocity offsetting calving, for Glacier 14 west
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Pinning ridge; velocity compensation of calving
